Half of the time lost to subway delays is caused by people, not trains

The subway lost — hours to — delays. — of that time came from security, medical, track-level and false-alarm incidents. This page answers two questions: where should the TTC add help, and when should a rider leave?

Would more staff help? Only for some causes

Security incidents: possiblyAfter the TTC added police, guards and ambassadors in 2023 and 2024, offences per million boardings fell, then returned near earlier levels by August 2025. No report links staffing to fewer delay minutes.
Track-level incidents: doors work betterThese are the longest delays of any cause. Platform edge doors sharply cut falls onto tracks in Hong Kong and Korea. The TTC paused its pilot in 2025 over cost.
Medical calls: speed mattersMany medical delays run long. New York posts EMTs at busy stations for this reason. Faster first response shortens the long ones.

This data can point to staffing but cannot prove it works. The next step is a measured pilot at the top station and window above, comparing delay minutes before and after against similar stations.

How it is built. Source: TTC Subway Delay Data since 2025, City of Toronto Open Data (Open Government Licence, Toronto), every row from 1 January 2025 to 31 August 2026. Kept only delays longer than zero minutes on Lines 1, 2 and 4. Station names were standardised (for example, Bloor and Yonge on Line 2 became Bloor-Yonge). TTC delay codes were grouped into ten plain-English causes; the grouping is my own. Charts follow IBCS conventions: titles state the finding, grey shows context, red marks the point. Every number is calculated live from the attached file and shows its source in Sources.
